(p. 3797, §1) — "stressed syllables (which is word-final) of sentence-medial words are marked by rising pitch accents, [L+H*] or [H*]" (p. 3797, Abstract) — "This tone is not categorized as a pitch accent because it surfaces on an unstressed, non-final syllable of a word. However, since the [Hi] syllable is slightly louder than adjacent syllables, this tone was proposed to be a prominence-marking tone." (p. 3797, §1.1)

However, since the [Hi] syllable is slightly louder than adja…
new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog (final syllable of the word) but the paper adds the exceptions (Russian loans, question words) and the optional word-initial [Hi] prominence tone that is post-lexical, not stress. Note the stress placement is credited to Comrie [2] (1997) rather than established instrumentally here; the paper is an AM intonation study that presupposes final stress. Byline is Royer & Jun, not Royer alone.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the last syllable of the morphological word (attributed to Comrie 1997), and the paper's whole intonational analysis treats the word-final syllable as the stressed syllable that hosts the L+H*/H* pitch accent (focused verbs carry the pitch accent 'on their final, stressed syllable', p. 3799). An optional post-lexical high tone [Hi] appears on the first (or second) syllable of a word; it is explicitly not a pitch accent and not lexical stress, but an edge-marking prominence tone compared to French 'initial stress'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: No secondary stress as such; the paper describes an optional word-initial [Hi] tone on an unstressed non-final syllable (slightly louder than adjacent syllables) that marks prominence at the left edge of a word/phrase, likened to the French initial accent (pp. 3797, 3800).
new_statements.exceptions: Loanwords from Russian and question words (citing Comrie 1997), p. 3797.
new_statements.identity_note: The paper is about Kazan (Volga) Tatar; data from six native speakers in Tatarstan, Russia, plus two Los Angeles-based native speakers (p. 3798).

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation (Poppe 1963 sec. 1.42, pp.14-15) is present verbatim in the held scanned at the stated place; page inference from the footer/running head matches the record's locator. (2) Deciding source is a descriptive reference grammar (1963) with a dedicated stress section, held in full; it is corroborated by the 2018 901-page reference grammar (Burbiel, now persisted under our files) and by an open instrumental intonation study (Royer & Jun 2018, downloaded now) showing the pitch accent docks on the word-final stressed syllable and on the lexically stressed syllable of Russian loans. All three agree on default word-final stress, last suffix wins, with a closed set of morphological exceptions (initial-stressed 2nd-person imperatives and interrogatives; pre-stressing predicative endings, negative -ma, 3pl present -lar, clitic particles; Russian loans). sources.quote: 'Comrie [1] notes that like other Turkic languages, stress in Tatar typically occurs on the last syllable of a morphological word, with some exceptions (e.g., loan words from Russian, question words).' Instrumentally: 'Typically, the stressed syllable of each content word is marked' by L+H* aligned with the (final) stressed syllable; words with exceptional non-final stress (Russian loan matras 'mattress', penult) show the H on the stressed syllable, i.e. the tone marks stress, not the word edge.
